lessons.title: Reading Candlesticks
intro: Every candlestick shows four prices for one time period: Open, High, Low and Close (OHLC). A 5-minute candle covers every trade between, say, 12:00 and 12:05.
The thick body spans from Open to Close. Green means price closed higher than it opened (open $100, close $105). Red means it closed lower.
The thin lines above and below the body are wicks. They show the highest and lowest prices reached before the candle closed.

questions.question: What does a green candlestick tell you?
options: Price closed higher than it opened.
Price closed lower than it opened, so sellers won.
Trading volume was above average.
Price will rise in the next candle.
questions.explanation: Green means the close is above the open. It describes the past, not the future.

questions.question: A candle opens at $50, reaches $55, dips to $48 and closes at $53. Where do the wicks end?
options: There are no wicks on a green candle.
Upper wick at $55, lower wick at $48.
Upper wick at $53, lower wick at $50.
Both wicks end at $51.50, the midpoint.
questions.explanation: The body runs from $50 (open) to $53 (close). The wicks stretch to the high of $55 and the low of $48.

questions.question: A red candle has a very long lower wick. What happened during that period?
options: No buyers traded at all.
Price closed at its lowest point.
Sellers pushed price down, then buyers lifted it off the lows.
The exchange reported a data error.
questions.explanation: A long lower wick means lower prices were rejected. Buyers absorbed the selling before the candle closed.

questions.question: How many prices does one candlestick summarise?
options: One: the close.
Two: open and close.
Three: the high, the low and the average price traded.
Four: open, high, low and close.
questions.explanation: A candle captures open, high, low and close (OHLC). Together they show who controlled that period.

lessons.title: Market Trends
intro: Prices move in waves, not straight lines. An uptrend makes higher highs and higher lows: each dip stops above the last one.
A downtrend is the mirror image: lower highs and lower lows. Each bounce fails below the previous peak.
When price swings between a clear ceiling and floor without new highs or lows, the market is sideways, also called a range.

questions.question: How does price usually behave in a sideways market?
options: It bounces between a horizontal floor and ceiling.
It rises steadily for weeks with almost no pullbacks along the way.
It sets a new record high every day.
It falls in a straight line.
questions.explanation: A sideways market has no clear direction. Price trades back and forth inside a range.

questions.question: BTC rises from $60,000 to $64,000, dips to $62,000, then climbs to $67,000. What structure is this?
options: A sideways range.
An uptrend: a higher low, then a higher high.
A downtrend reversal.
No structure at all.
questions.explanation: The dip held above the start ($62,000 > $60,000) and the next peak was higher ($67,000 > $64,000). That is an uptrend.

questions.question: Which is a key structural warning that an uptrend may be ending?
options: Volume is slightly lower on a holiday.
A single red candle appears on a 1-minute chart during the move.
Price breaks below the most recent higher low.
Price touches a round number like $50,000.
questions.explanation: Breaking the last higher low breaks the uptrend pattern. It shows buyers failed to defend their previous floor.

questions.question: In a clear downtrend, what does a disciplined beginner usually avoid?
options: Waiting on the sidelines until the structure clearly changes.
Studying where the last lower high formed.
Practising with small paper trades.
Buying every dip expecting an instant turnaround.
questions.explanation: Buying every dip means fighting the trend, which often leads to repeated losses. Staying out is also a valid decision.

lessons.title: Support and Resistance
intro: Support is a price floor where buyers stepped in before. Traders remember those bounces and place buy orders there again.
Resistance is a price ceiling where sellers stepped in before. Price stalls there as traders take profit or sell.
When price breaks clearly through a level and holds, the old ceiling often becomes the new floor. If it quickly falls back, it was a false breakout.

questions.question: What is a false breakout?
options: A breakout that happens on a weekend.
A breakout announced in the news.
Price pokes through a level, then quickly falls back inside.
Any breakout above $100.
questions.explanation: A false breakout briefly crosses a level and then reverses. It traps traders who bought the moment price crossed.

questions.question: SOL has risen to $150 four times this week and failed to close above it each time. What is $150?
options: Support.
Resistance.
A stop loss.
A guaranteed breakout point.
questions.explanation: Repeated rejection from above marks resistance. Sellers keep appearing at $150.

questions.question: Price breaks above resistance at $100 and holds there for several candles. What often happens on the next dip?
options: $100 may now act as support.
Price must fall back to $50.
The level stops mattering forever.
Resistance moves up to $200 automatically.
questions.explanation: Broken resistance often turns into support. Traders who missed the breakout may buy the retest.

questions.question: Why does price often react at old support levels?
options: Exchanges automatically block trading at prices below a support level.
Algorithms only trade round numbers.
Support is set by regulators each day.
Many traders remember the level and place orders there.
questions.explanation: Levels work because people act on them. Clustered buy orders at a remembered price can slow or reverse a fall.

lessons.title: The Stop Loss
intro: A stop loss is an order that closes your trade automatically at a price you set in advance. It caps how much one trade can cost you.
Put the stop beyond the level that proves your idea wrong. Buying at $50 because $48 is support? Your stop belongs just below $48, not at a random number.
Never move a stop further away once the trade is open. A planned $3 loss can quietly grow into a $10 or $20 loss.
In fast markets price can jump past your stop, so the exit may be worse than planned. A stop still beats having no exit at all.

questions.question: Why is trading without a stop loss risky?
options: Brokers charge an extra fee on every order placed without a stop.
Take-profit orders stop working.
It is against the rules of paper trading.
A small loss can grow into a large one with no planned exit.
questions.explanation: Without a stop, nothing limits the loss except your own nerve. Sharp moves can do a lot of damage before you react.

questions.question: What is the main job of a stop loss?
options: Limit the loss when the trade idea is proven wrong.
Guarantee that every trade you open ends with at least a small profit.
Borrow more money from the platform.
Lower trading fees.
questions.explanation: A stop loss protects your account by exiting when your reason for the trade no longer holds.

questions.question: You buy at $50 because support sits at $48. Where does your stop belong?
options: At $52, above your entry.
Just below $48, around $47.
At $30, to give it lots of room.
Nowhere, if you feel confident.
questions.explanation: If price breaks below $48 support, your reason for buying is gone. The stop goes just beyond that level.

questions.question: A trader buys at $100 with a stop at $95. Price drops to $96 and they move the stop to $90. What is this?
options: A trailing stop.
Smart rebalancing.
Avoiding a loss by risking a bigger one.
Dollar-cost averaging.
questions.explanation: Moving the stop away doubles the planned risk from $5 to $10 per unit. It is driven by hope, not by the chart.

lessons.title: Position Sizing
intro: Many experienced traders risk only a small fixed share of their account per trade, often around 1%. On a $10,000 account, that is $100.
Size comes from your stop distance: size = money at risk ÷ stop distance. Risking $100 with a stop $2 away means 50 units.
Example: buy at $50, stop at $48. $100 ÷ $2 = 50 units. If the stop is hit, you lose about $100, not your whole account.
At 1% risk, ten losses in a row cost about 10% of the account. At 20% risk, the same streak would leave you with about 11%.

questions.question: With a $10,000 account and a 1% risk rule, what is the most you plan to lose on one trade?
questions.explanation: 1% of $10,000 is $100. If the stop is hit, the loss should be about $100.

questions.question: You risk $100. Entry is $50, stop is $48. How many units do you buy?
options: 200 units
50 units
500 units
25 units
questions.explanation: $100 ÷ $2 stop distance = 50 units. If price hits $48 you lose $100.

questions.question: Your stop has to be twice as far away as usual. What should happen to your position size?
options: Double it.
Keep it the same, because size and stop distance are unrelated.
Halve it, so the money at risk stays the same.
Skip the stop instead.
questions.explanation: A wider stop means more loss per unit. Halving the size keeps the total risk at your fixed amount.

questions.question: A beginner with $5,000 opens a $50,000 position using 10x leverage. Price moves 10% against them. What happens?
options: They lose $500.
Leverage cancels the loss.
The broker pays half the loss.
They lose about $5,000, the whole account.
questions.explanation: 10% of $50,000 is $5,000, which is the entire account. Leverage multiplies losses as well as gains.

lessons.title: Trading Mindset
intro: In the EU, brokers offering CFDs (a leveraged product) must publish how many retail accounts lose money. The figures are commonly above 70%.
One winning trade proves little. A trade with no plan can win by luck; skill shows up as a repeatable process over many trades.
Revenge trading means jumping into a bigger, rushed trade right after a loss to win it back. It usually turns one loss into several.
FOMO, the fear of missing out, pushes you to chase a price that already spiked. A missed move costs nothing; chasing one can.

questions.question: You just lost $200. You feel angry and want to open a trade twice your usual size right away. What is this?
options: Smart recovery planning.
Revenge trading.
Position sizing.
A trailing stop.
questions.explanation: Trading bigger out of anger to win back a loss is revenge trading. Taking a break is usually the better move.

questions.question: What do EU broker disclosures show about retail CFD accounts?
options: Fewer than 10% lose money.
Commonly more than 70% lose money.
About half lose money, as you would expect from a coin flip.
Almost nobody loses money.
questions.explanation: Brokers must publish this figure, and it is commonly above 70%. Losing is the norm, which is why process and risk control matter.

questions.question: A coin jumps 200% in an hour and you feel you must buy now. What is the disciplined response?
options: Buy right away with your whole account before it climbs higher.
Borrow money to buy more.
Notice the FOMO and wait for a clear setup with a stop.
Short it with 50x leverage.
questions.explanation: Chasing a vertical move often means buying near the top. Waiting for structure lets you define your risk.

questions.question: You buy with no plan and no stop because it 'feels right', and make 15%. What is the honest lesson?
options: The result was good, but the process was poor, so it was likely luck.
Gut feeling is a reliable strategy.
Stops are unnecessary.
You should repeat it with a bigger size.
questions.explanation: A profit does not prove a good decision. Repeating a no-plan trade eventually leads to large losses.
